articles.title: Exames gratuitos de próstata e mamografia em Campo Grande e MS | G1
articles.standfirst: Atendimentos são realizados no Hospital de Câncer Alfredo Abrão, com distribuição diária de senhas. Em Dourados, Hospital Universitário também oferece exames de PSA durante a programação do Novembro Azul.
articles.summary: Hospital de Câncer e HU-UFGD oferecem exames gratuitos de próstata e mamografia em Campo Grande e Dourados até sexta-feira com distribuição diária de senhas.
articles.body:
Hospital de Câncer Alfredo Abrão, em Campo Grande (MS) — Foto: Divulgação

Moradores de Campo Grande podem fazer exames gratuitos de prevenção ao câncer de próstata e de mama até sexta-feira (27). A ação é realizada pelo Hospital de Câncer Alfredo Abrão e faz parte das campanhas Outubro Rosa e Novembro Azul, que incentivam o diagnóstico precoce das doenças.

No hospital, são distribuídas diariamente 100 senhas para exames de PSA, voltados à avaliação da saúde da próstata, e outras 80 para mamografias. O atendimento ocorre de segunda a sexta-feira, exceto feriados, e não há cobrança pelos exames.

Para conseguir uma vaga, é necessário chegar ao hospital nos horários de distribuição das senhas: a partir das 5h para o PSA e das 6h para a mamografia. Os interessados devem apresentar RG, CPF e cartão do SUS.

Quem pode fazer os exames em Campo Grande?

De acordo com as informações divulgadas pelo hospital, a mamografia é oferecida a mulheres com idade entre 40 e 74 anos. Já o exame de PSA é destinado a homens de 45 a 75 anos.

O PSA é feito por meio de uma coleta de sangue e mede uma proteína produzida pela próstata. Alterações nos níveis podem indicar problemas como inflamações, aumento benigno da próstata ou câncer, mas não confirmam, sozinhas, a existência da doença.

Local: Hospital de Câncer Alfredo Abrão, em Campo Grande.

Mamografia: 80 senhas por dia, distribuídas a partir das 6h.

PSA: 100 senhas por dia, distribuídas a partir das 5h.

Dias: de segunda a sexta-feira, exceto finais de semana e feriados.

Endereço: Rua Marechal Rondon, 1053, em Campo Grande.

Exames de PSA também são oferecidos em Dourados

Em Dourados, o Hospital Universitário da Universidade Federal da Grande Dourados (HU-UFGD) também iniciou uma programação especial do Novembro Azul nesta segunda-feira (23). A unidade prevê a realização de aproximadamente 250 exames gratuitos de PSA até sexta-feira (27).

As coletas são feitas das 7h às 10h. Não é necessário agendar: o atendimento ocorre por ordem de chegada, mas as vagas são limitadas.

Os interessados devem procurar as salas 12 ou 17 da Unidade da Mulher e da Criança (UMC), onde passam por uma triagem e são encaminhados para a coleta de sangue no próprio hospital.

Podem fazer o exame homens a partir de 50 anos, aqueles entre 45 e 49 anos que tenham fatores de risco, como histórico familiar de câncer de próstata, e pessoas que apresentem sintomas urinários, como dificuldade para urinar, jato fraco ou interrompido e aumento da frequência urinária.

Como se preparar para o PSA em Dourados?

Evitar relações sexuais nas 72 horas anteriores ao exame;

Não andar de bicicleta, motocicleta ou a cavalo.

Os resultados serão entregues no sábado (28), quando também haverá consultas com a equipe de Urologia, das 7h às 12h. Por isso, os pacientes que fizerem a coleta durante a semana precisam retornar ao hospital nessa data.

O HU-UFGD fica na Rua Ivo Alves da Rocha, 558, no bairro Altos do Indaiá, em Dourados. A entrada para os atendimentos é pela Unidade da Mulher e da Criança (UMC).

articles.title: Rekha Patra, BJP MLA from Hingalganj, on ventilator, mystery over cause
articles.summary: BJP Hingalganj MLA Rekha Patra hospitalized in Kolkata with suspected poisoning or food poisoning; on ventilator as tests probe possible organophosphate exposure.
articles.body: KOLKATA: Rekha Patra, BJP’s Hingalganj MLA and one of the prominent faces of “female victimhood” that emerged from the Sandeshkhali movement when Trinamool was in office, was admitted to a private hospital off EM Bypass early on Sunday with “symptoms of poisoning”. She is on ventilator.State health minister Sharadwat Mukherjee, who visited the hospital in the morning, said Patra suffered “food poisoning”. “She is doing well and responding... to treatment. Hopefully, she will recover soon,” he said.Cops from North 24 Parganas, however, said the family had reportedly told the hospital she had “ingested a herbal larvicide”. The larvicide is suspected to contain organophosphate, a chemical commonly found in agricultural pesticides and insecticides.Sandip Patra, the MLA’s husband, and BJP seniors in North 24 Parganas did not speak on the issue.Rekha fell ill around 9pm on Saturday at her home in Hingalganj, near Sandeshkhali. She was taken to a local hospital before being shifted to Basirhat Super Speciality Hospital, where she was treated for nearly four hours. As her condition did not improve significantly, doctors referred her to Kolkata. She was adm-itted to the private hospital off EM Bypass around 3am.“The referral card reportedly mentioned that Rekha Patra was drowsy and responding poorly to verbal instructions. Doctors attempted to revive her by applying pressure to her chest, but there was little response. At the time, her blood pressure was recorded at 124/70, while her pulse rate was 110 beats per minute. She also required oxygen support at four litres per minute,” a source at the city hospital said.At the Basirhat hospital, doctors treated her for suspected poisoning, administering six activated charcoal tablets, and atropine and pralidoxime injections. “They tried to extract the suspected toxic substance through a tube inserted through her nose. Medicines for vomiting and gastric problems, along with antibiotics, were given,” an official at the hospital said.Health minister Mukherjee said after visiting the Kolkata hospital, “She is much more stable than when she was brought in. Her family has spoken with CM Suvendu Adhikari and she was brought to Kolkata for treatment... Poisoning has not been confirmed yet. She fell ill after eating at night. Samples have been sent for testing. We will have to wait for the reports.”Rekha — who hit the headlines ahead of the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, when she led a movement for around two months against alleged rape, torture and land-grab in Sandeshkhali — has of late been facing a rough time in her neighbourhood and her party. She won this year’s assembly polls from Hingalganj, defeating her closest rival (Debes Mandal of Trinamool Congress) by 4,712 votes.Rekha has been mired in controversies, including allegations of land-grab, since being elected as an MLA. In Aug, a monk from Hingalganj lodged a complaint with CM Adhikari at Janatar Darbar against her.Keshabananda Maharaj, a resident of Lebukhali in Hingalganj, alleged that the MLA had taken on rent 12 rooms in his house in March, but had paid only two months’ rent since. She had allegedly promised to buy the house — spread across four bighas — for Rs 1.25 crore, but went back on her commitment. In Sept, Rekha was accused of grabbing around nine bighas of agricultural land from a farmer’s family.A few days ago, she had publicly expressed resentment against several BJP seniors in North 24 Parganas, alleging that she was not invited to district-level events and was humiliated at public programmes over her educational qualifications. She had also reportedly approached BJP’s state leadership several times over the alleged mistreatment.Several prominent Trinamool faces from the Sandeshkhali area, including Sheikh Shahjahan, Shibaprasad Hazra and Uttam Sardar, are now facing trial following allegations of rape, torture and land-grab first voiced by Rekha in Feb 2024.Another face of victimhood during the Trinamool regime, BJP MLA Ratna Debnath, the mother of the RG Kar rape-murder victim, has also been in news recently following her outbursts after the death of BJP worker Prasenjit Das in her constituency, Panihati. “It would have been better had BJP not won this time,” an anguished Debnath said on Nov 17, prompting many BJP seniors to call her “immature”.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Kolkata | Silver Rate in Kolkata | Bank Holidays in Kolkata | Public Holidays in Kolkata | Kolkata AQI | Weather in Kolkata | Petrol Price in Kolkata | Diesel Price in Kolkata | CNG Price in Kolkata | LPG Price in KolkataStay updated with the latest Kolkata news. articles.title: Can AI spot breast cancer earlier? NHS launches world's largest trial to find out
articles.summary: Researchers will test the technology in breast cancer screening which could ease pressure on the NHS.
articles.body:
Nearly 700,000 women across the UK are to be invited to join the world's largest trial of how artificial intelligence can help in breast cancer screening.

AI will be used to review mammograms to see if it can improve early cancer detection and ease the workload of clinical staff, while not over-diagnosing women unnecessarily.

Recruitment to the EDITH trial has already begun at Cambridge University Hospitals, the first of 30 sites across the UK.

Women aged 50 to 71 are invited for routine breast screening every three years in the UK, and more than two million attend annually.

At present two NHS experts look at each breast X-ray, known as a mammogram, but in the trial, one of the human readers will be replaced by AI.

Several smaller studies have already shown that AI can improve breast cancer detection rates, but researchers running this trial say they need to be sure it won't cause harm by leading to women being recalled unnecessarily for further tests.

Sian Taylor-Phillips, professor of population health at the University of Warwick, and co-chief investigator said: "AI-assisted technology could help improve early cancer detection but we want to avoid the overdiagnosis of milder disease that would never have caused symptoms."

Breast cancer is the most common cancer among women in the UK, with around 59,000 cases diagnosed each year.

About a third of these are picked up by routine mammograms, usually at an early stage when they can be more easily treated.

It's estimated the screening programme helps prevent around 1,300 deaths a year.

Prof Fiona Gilbert, department of radiology, University of Cambridge, honorary consultant at Addenbrooke's Hospital, and co-chief investigator said: "Millions of women have a mammogram each year and only a small number, less than 1%, will have cancer.

"Technology can make reviewing these images more efficient, freeing up specialist breast radiologists to spend more time caring for patients with cancer, supporting faster diagnosis and earlier treatment."

Gilbert told the BBC there was a "huge shortfall" in radiologists and that the number of imaging examinations was increasing by 8% a year.

Shirley Essex, 70, from Cambridgeshire, was diagnosed with early-stage breast cancer a year ago after a routine screening appointment.

She had surgery and radiotherapy, but did not require chemotherapy.

She told the BBC that her mammogram had saved her life: "I was astonished to be told I had cancer because I did not have any symptoms."

Shirley is not part of the study but is passionate about the importance of screening.

"I feel so lucky my cancer was detected early. It was my last routine mammogram, so if I had not attended, my cancer would have kept growing," she said.

Women will be informed about the study when they receive a routine screening invitation, but will not be obliged to take part.

The trial will not change what happens during a breast screening appointment.

Instead, it will test whether AI-assisted tools could replace one of the two human specialists reviewing mammograms.

Researchers say machine-learning software can be trained on millions of previous images in order to detect patterns, and so potentially find subtle changes in breast tissue that might be missed by the human eye.

In one arm of the trial, an AI programme will grade images before they are sent to NHS experts. In another, it will review images afterwards.

The £11m trial is funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR).

It is being led by the University of Warwick, the University of Cambridge and Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, working with NHS England.

On a visit to the breast screening unit at Addenbrooke's Hospital, Health Secretary Yvette Cooper told the BBC: "AI has huge potential to improve treatment, which is why we need trials like this to ensure we are using it in the most effective way with proper safeguards."

Prof Peter Johnson, national clinical director for cancer at NHS England, said NHS breast screening "saves lives" and he urged every woman invited to the trial to take part.

"Every scan will still be seen by a specialist, and if proven effective, it could ensure women get the diagnosis and treatment they need sooner," he said.

Four AI companies are involved in the trial, which is expected to last around three years.

articles.title: Las personas nacidas entre 1960 y 1970 son la última generación que tuvo una infancia feliz, según el psicólogo Peter Gray
articles.standfirst: El experto vincula el auge de la ansiedad infantil con la pérdida del juego libre
articles.summary: El experto vincula el auge de la ansiedad infantil con la pérdida del juego libre
articles.body: Tardes enteras en la calle, bicicletas sin rumbo, juegos inventados sobre la marcha y padres que solo pedían una cosa: volver a casa antes de cenar. Para muchos adultos, estos recuerdos forman parte de una infancia que hoy parece de otro planeta. Y, según un reconocido psicólogo estadounidense, esa diferencia podría tener más importancia de la que creemos. Peter Gray, profesor investigador de Psicología y Neurociencia en el Boston College, sostiene que quienes nacieron entre 1960 y 1970 fueron los últimos en crecer con una libertad que las generaciones posteriores han ido perdiendo. Para Gray, lo que marcó aquella infancia no fue la ausencia de problemas, sino la autonomía. Los niños jugaban, exploraban y resolvían conflictos sin supervisión constante. A través de ese juego libre, explica, aprendían a ganar confianza, a hacer amigos y a enfrentarse a dificultades por sí mismos. Incluso el juego con cierto riesgo, como trepar a lo alto de un árbol, tenía un papel protector. Según sus trabajos, ayuda a prevenir fobias y reduce la ansiedad futura al reforzar la seguridad del niño para afrontar situaciones complicadas. En 2023, Gray publicó junto a los investigadores David Lancy y David Bjorklund un artículo en The Journal of Pediatrics que resumía las pruebas de esta tesis. Su conclusión: una de las principales causas del aumento de la ansiedad, la depresión y el suicidio entre niños y adolescentes es el descenso continuado, durante décadas, de sus oportunidades para jugar y moverse sin la vigilancia de los adultos. Según los autores, ese afán por guiar y proteger a los menores, aunque bienintencionado, los ha privado de la independencia que necesitan. Un ejemplo: en 2014, el recreo en las escuelas de primaria de Estados Unidos duraba de media menos de 27 minutos al día. Además, Gray no culpa principalmente a los móviles ni a las redes sociales, sino a una infancia cada vez más organizada por escuelas y familias.

articles.title: Northern Ireland doctors begin fresh strike over pay dispute
articles.summary: It follows a separate 24-hour strike on Friday in which resident doctors took industrial action as part of the same dispute.
articles.body:
Consultants and specialist doctors have begun a 24-hour strike as part of an ongoing dispute over pay.

It follows a separate 24-hour strike on Friday in which resident doctors took industrial action as part of the same dispute.

The British Medical Association (BMA) rejected a recommended 3.5% pay rise and wants to restore the value of doctors' pay to 2008 levels.

Health Minister Robbie Butler said he had accepted the recommended rise but could not implement it without sufficient funding for his department.

Niall Corrigan, a consultant psychiatrist in the Belfast Trust, was among those on the picket line outside the Ulster Hospital.

He said they were on strike "to advocate for the health service", which he said had been "under-resourced" in recent years.

He said he sympathised with patients who have appointments during the strike but if they did not take action then there would be "continuing degradation of our health service".

Leeanne Davison also works in the Belfast Trust as an associate specialist doctor in ICU.

She said doctors in Northern Ireland were "quite rightly feeling aggrieved that their colleagues across the UK have already had uplift in their pay awards".

"Most public and private sector workers are now back in line with inflation, yet doctors, nurses and hospital staff are not," she said.

She added that her colleagues could not "continue to watch the health service disintegrate around us".

"We can no longer accept the moral injury of trying to deliver the care that we want to deliver in third world conditions, delivering care to patients in corridors," she said.

The strike, which began at 07:00 GMT, has taken the form of Christmas Day cover meaning full emergency cover will remain in place.

The health minister said his door remained open.

"But, to be clear, going beyond the 3.5% as recommended by the independent pay review body would have significant repercussions for nurses, teachers, police officers and indeed the entire public sector workforce," he added.

The Western and South Eastern health trusts have asked patients with appointments on Monday to attend as planned, unless their trust tells them otherwise.

The South Eastern Trust said the urgent care centre at Lagan Valley Hospital would be closed on Monday, and that postponed appointments and procedures would be rescheduled as soon as possible.

Dr David Farren, chair of the BMA's Northern Ireland consultants committee, told Good Morning Ulster that doctors were not being valued in Northern Ireland.

"We have given the trusts a six week notice period, which is six times longer than the legal requirement, so they can plan for that," he said.

"We met with the minster on 1 October, any sort of meaningful engagement could've halted these strikes, after that meeting we heard nothing.

"No doctor wishes to strike, we are incredibly sorry that it has come to this."

He said full emergency cover would remain in place, but "hospital appointments, routine investigations, routine operating lists" would be affected.

Dr Farren said the official advice was that "if you have not been notified, you go ahead to your appointment.

"However don't be surprised if your appointment doesn't happen when you get there," he added.

The health minister said Monday's strike, paired with Friday's would have "real consequences for patients, waiting lists and service delivery, with around 1,694 patients expected to be impacted".

He also warned there would be further consequences for patients "as we head into the busy winter period due to the knock-on effect of the strikes as we reschedule cancelled activity".

The Department of Health has said implementing the 2026-27 pay award and Real Living Wage would cost about £280m.

Butler said his "real pressure" was trying to deliver the Real Living Wage for domiciliary workers delivering care packages at home.

Sinn Féin assembly member Philip McGuigan, who is chair of Stormont's health committee, told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme he understood there would be "many disappointed and, in some cases, angry patients".

"Nobody wants to see strike action, nobody wants to see patients missing appointments, particularly given the length of the waiting list, but what I do believe the (health) minister needs to do is engage meaningfully with the BMA," he said.

articles.title: Vizag man, 61, undergoes cataract surgery, suffers prolonged pain and vision loss, consumer commission orders hospital to pay Rs 9L compensation, refund Rs 8,020 with 6% interest and Rs 21,000 costs
articles.summary: VISAKHAPATNAM: The District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission has directed a private eye hospital in Visakhapatnam to pay Rs 9 lakh as compensation
articles.body: VISAKHAPATNAM: The District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission has directed a private eye hospital in Visakhapatnam to pay Rs 9 lakh as compensation to a 61-year-old man after holding it responsible for negligence during and after a cataract operation that led to prolonged suffering and deterioration in his vision.The commission also ordered Visakha Eye Hospital, managed by Visakha Nethra Jyothi Pvt Ltd, to refund Rs 8,020 spent by the patient on the procedure, with 6% annual interest from June 7, 2021, and pay Rs 21,000 towards litigation costs. The hospital has been given one month to comply. If it fails to pay the compensation within the stipulated period, the amount will attract 9% annual interest from the date of default.The order was pronounced on November 16, 2026, in a complaint filed by Vasam Hari Krishna, a container driver from Madhurawada, who alleged that the hospital’s treatment had damaged his left eye and affected his ability to earn a living. The commission dismissed the complaint against National Insurance Company, which had provided professional indemnity cover to the hospital’s doctors.Patient alleged complications during surgeryAccording to the complaint, Hari Krishna approached the hospital on June 5, 2021, after experiencing a decline in vision in his left eye. Doctors advised cataract surgery. He said he wanted the procedure under the government’s Aarogyasri scheme, but the hospital declined, following which he agreed to pay Rs 11,500 towards the operation and Rs 900 for anaesthesia.The surgery was performed on June 7, 2021, by Dr Ramya. Hari Krishna alleged that anaesthesia was not administered and that the vacuum and water pumps were not functioning during the procedure. He also alleged that the doctor used a water bottle kept for drinking to clean his eye.He said he experienced severe pain through the night and returned to the hospital the next day. According to his complaint, doctors found that the eye had not been cleaned properly and that dust particles remained in it. He subsequently underwent another procedure on June 11 under the Aarogyasri scheme.The hospital denied negligence, stating that the surgery was conducted according to accepted medical practices and that a fragment of the cataract nucleus had dropped into the vitreous cavity, a recognised complication of cataract surgery. It said a retina specialist performed a vitrectomy on June 11 to remove the fragment.Commission points to discrepancies in medical recordsHari Krishna later approached the hospital again in January 2022 after experiencing blurred vision and coloured halos. He was diagnosed with retinal detachment in the left eye. The hospital said he was advised to undergo retinal surgery on January 12 but did not return for it.He subsequently visited LV Prasad Eye Institute, where doctors reportedly advised immediate surgery, warning that his vision could be lost. He underwent an operation there on January 18, 2022.The consumer commission, while examining the medical records, noted discrepancies between two reports issued by the hospital on June 5 and June 9, 2021, which recorded different findings on his vision within a span of four days. It said these discrepancies supported the patient’s allegations about the failure of the initial procedure.The commission also criticised the hospital for initially taking the stand that the relevant record could not be traced and producing it later during the proceedings. It said the hospital’s handling of medical records reflected a lack of proper maintenance and an unfair approach during the adjudication process.Holding the hospital responsible for deficiency in service, the commission said the patient had been made to endure pain and suffering and had to pursue a legal battle for nearly three years. It said the compensation was based on the principles of justice, equity and fairness.The complaint had sought a refund of Rs 8,020 with 24% interest and Rs 20 lakh in compensation. The commission partly allowed it, awarding Rs 9 lakh in compensation, the refund with 6% interest and Rs 21,000 in costs. articles.title: Popular bedroom supplements often fail to deliver, says longevity physician
articles.summary: Dr. Pablo Prichard shares why most sexual enhancement supplements fail and how L-arginine and L-citrulline may help blood flow and erectile dysfunction.
articles.body: Pharmacy aisles and social media feeds are crowded with capsules, powders and gummies promising to boost libido and sexual performance. Yet according to physicians and clinical research, most over-the-counter sexual enhancement products are ineffective — and some carry health risks. It's a mistake to treat all sexual health concerns as a single problem, according to Dr. Pablo Prichard, an Arizona-based surgeon who focuses on longevity and preventative health. Before reaching for a bottle, patients should understand the difference between low sex drive and physical performance issues like erectile dysfunction or vaginal dryness, he told Fox News Digital. WHY STACKING SUPPLEMENTS WITHOUT A BLOOD TEST FIRST CAN DO MORE HARM THAN GOOD "When you're looking at supplements, you have to think, ‘Is this supplement affecting what my problem is individually?’" Prichard said. "Because if you have a hormonal issue, and you take a supplement that supposedly increases your blood flow, that doesn't necessarily improve your condition." If performance issues stem from restricted circulation, certain amino acids may offer modest support. Supplements like L-arginine and L-citrulline target the nitric oxide pathway, which helps relax and widen blood vessels, Prichard said. According to Cleveland Clinic, L-citrulline converts into L-arginine in the body to boost nitric oxide production, and small clinical studies suggest it may help improve mild erectile dysfunction. VIAGRA COULD DO MORE THAN ADVERTISED AS STUDY REVEALS SURPRISING HEALTH SUPERPOWER Still, the clinic notes that overall scientific evidence remains mixed, larger clinical trials are needed, and the supplements are less reliable than prescription treatments. "If you actually have a blood-flow issue, then taking a supplement like this … that improves your blood flow could actually help," Prichard said. "If you don't have a blood-flow issue, and it's another problem, then taking a supplement like this probably won't help." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ While certain herbal extracts, such as Panax ginseng and saffron, have shown potential in small trials to improve erectile function and sexual satisfaction, experts urge caution with unregulated sexual enhancement blends. "The FDA has repeatedly seen actual Viagra in these 'herbal Viagra' medications," Prichard said. Laboratory testing by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has identified hundreds of over-the-counter products marketed as "all-natural" sexual enhancers that secretly contain prescription drug ingredients — most commonly sildenafil (the active ingredient in Viagra) and tadalafil (found in Cialis). Because these hidden drugs aren't listed on the label, the agency warns that consumers risk dangerous side effects or severe drops in blood pressure, particularly if they take heart medications containing nitrates. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Taking unknown doses of prescription erectile dysfunction drugs can trigger dangerous side effects. Prichard warned that combining hidden sildenafil — or even high doses of L-arginine — with heart medications like nitroglycerin or hypertension drugs can cause life-threatening drops in blood pressure. Similarly, mixing herbs like ginkgo biloba with blood thinners can elevate bleeding risks. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER For both men and women experiencing low desire or dryness tied to shifting hormone levels, consulting with a physician is more effective than guessing at the store, the doctor advised. Any new or worsening changes in sexual function warrant a medical checkup, as they could be a warning sign of cardiovascular disease, diabetes or depression. "I think a lot of times, people take the easy way out and say, 'Yeah, I have this problem, I'm just going to take this pill ... and that's going to fix my problem,'" Prichard said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Foundational habits like prioritizing sleep, managing stress and getting both aerobic and strength exercise "can have a much bigger influence on your sexual health than just taking a supplement," the doctor added.

articles.title: Google AI smartwatch could flag high blood pressure
articles.summary: Google's AI used smartwatch sensors to spot hypertension without a blood pressure cuff, but the Nature study found it missed about 1 in 3 cases.
articles.body: When was the last time you checked your blood pressure? If you're like a lot of people, it probably happened during your last doctor's appointment. And if you feel perfectly healthy, you may not give it another thought. That's what makes high blood pressure so concerning. You can have it for years without noticing anything wrong. Now, Google researchers are exploring a way to uncover that hidden danger using something many of us already wear on our wrists. In a new study recently published in Nature, researchers demonstrated an artificial intelligence system that can identify signs of hypertension using standard smartwatch sensors. It works in the background without requiring calibration with a traditional blood pressure cuff. The technology uses sensors that already exist in consumer smartwatches. That could make early detection much more accessible. However, the research also reveals a limitation that anyone relying on a smartwatch for health information should understand. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. SMARTWATCH AFIB ALERT SENDS DAD TO ER BEFORE HEART SURGERY How Google AI detects high blood pressure using a smartwatch Your smartwatch already knows quite a bit about your body. It can track your heart rate throughout the day. Depending on the model, it may also detect irregular heart rhythms. Google's new AI takes the information collected by those sensors and looks for signs of something harder to detect: ongoing high blood pressure. According to Google Research, the system analyzes two types of sensor data. Your smartwatch can pick up signals you cannot feel The first sensor uses light to detect changes in blood volume beneath your skin. It's the same basic technology many watches use to monitor your pulse. The second sensor measures movement. Researchers found that it can also capture incredibly small vibrations caused by your heart pumping blood. You wouldn't notice those vibrations. However, the AI can analyze them alongside your pulse patterns to look for signs associated with hypertension. The system collects information over multiple days. It then combines those patterns with your height to estimate the likelihood of sustained high blood pressure. Unlike a traditional monitor, the smartwatch doesn't produce a reading such as 120 over 80. Instead, it looks for signs that your blood pressure may be consistently elevated. What's interesting is that you wouldn't have to do anything differently. You could go about your day while your smartwatch quietly looks for potential warning signs. Google's smartwatch AI study reveals promising results Google worked with researchers from Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School to develop and test the system. First, researchers trained the underlying AI using nearly 500,000 hours of smartwatch sensor data collected from 2,109 consenting participants. They then evaluated the hypertension detection system in a clinical study involving 196 participants across five U.S. locations. None of those participants had known cardiovascular disease or were taking blood pressure medication. During the study, participants wore a consumer smartwatch for seven days. Researchers compared the AI's findings with results from 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring. That medical test uses a cuff to measure blood pressure repeatedly throughout the day and night. Doctors use it to help confirm hypertension. How accurate was Google's smartwatch AI? During initial screening, the results showed: For comparison, initial blood pressure screenings performed in medical offices identified 55.3% of participants with hypertension in the study. That's an encouraging result. However, the difference between the smartwatch and office screening was not statistically significant, according to a Nature Portfolio summary of the findings. There's another number worth paying attention to. The AI missed roughly one in three participants who had hypertension during initial screening. That's a number worth paying attention to. After all, we're talking about a condition that can lead to a heart attack or stroke, often without any warning signs. Researchers also looked at a smaller group of 48 people who had elevated blood pressure readings during their initial doctor's visit. In that group, the AI correctly identified 78.4% of those with ongoing hypertension. It also correctly ruled out the condition in 90.9% of those who didn't have it. Those results are encouraging, but there's still work to do. Google needs to test the technology on more people before we can know how reliably it can detect high blood pressure. MICROSOFT AI BEATS DOCTORS IN SIMULATED DIAGNOSIS TEST Can your Pixel Watch detect high blood pressure today? Here's where things get interesting for people who already own a Google smartwatch. Google introduced its Health Guardian features in September 2026. Among them is a blood pressure trends feature available through the Google Health app. According to Google's September announcement, blood pressure trends are available at no additional subscription cost on eligible Pixel Watch 3, Pixel Watch 4 and Pixel Watch 5 devices. Availability depends on your region. The feature analyzes pulse and movement patterns over time. Then, it provides a monthly assessment of whether your blood pressure trend appears high. Google says these existing Health Guardian capabilities are informed by clinical research, including work connected to its newly published findings. However, there's an important difference between the experimental system described in Nature and the feature available on your watch today. Google's current blood pressure feature has limitations The existing Pixel Watch feature is intended for general wellness. Google specifically says it cannot diagnose hypertension or serve as a medical screening tool. It also cannot tell you your actual systolic or diastolic blood pressure numbers. According to Google's support documentation, the feature provides a monthly trend assessment such as "High" or "Not high." And a "Not high" result doesn't guarantee your blood pressure is normal. Google also warns users against relying on these estimates to change medications or treatment plans. Meanwhile, the newly published research remains exploratory. Google has not announced that the experimental hypertension screening system will become a commercial diagnostic feature. Apple Watch already offers hypertension alerts Google has some competition in this area. Apple has already introduced FDA-cleared hypertension notifications for compatible Apple Watch models. As we previously reported in Apple Watch gets FDA-approved hypertension alerts, the feature looks for patterns associated with chronic high blood pressure. It uses information gathered by the watch's optical heart sensor over 30-day periods. The feature supports Apple Watch Series 9 and later models, along with Apple Watch Ultra 2 and later models, subject to software and regional availability. If the watch detects concerning patterns, it can notify you. However, Apple also makes clear that the feature cannot diagnose hypertension. And it may miss cases. Apple recommends checking your blood pressure with a traditional cuff and discussing the results with a healthcare professional if you receive an alert. So, while Apple and Google are approaching this technology differently, the current guidance remains clear. A smartwatch alert can give you useful information, but you still need an accurate blood pressure measurement. Why detecting high blood pressure earlier could save lives High blood pressure has earned the nickname "silent killer" for a reason. According to the World Health Organization, more than one billion adults worldwide live with hypertension. Many have no idea they have it. Meanwhile, untreated high blood pressure can damage blood vessels and increase the risk of a heart attack or stroke. Younger adults can be particularly vulnerable to missed diagnoses because they may feel healthy and see little reason to get checked. Now, consider what could happen if a smartwatch noticed concerning patterns before someone developed symptoms. That person might decide to schedule an appointment and have their blood pressure checked. If doctors confirm hypertension, earlier treatment could help reduce the risk of complications. Of course, researchers still need to determine whether smartwatch-based screening actually improves diagnosis rates and long-term health outcomes. COULD A PAINT-ON ELECTRONIC TATTOO SPOT HEART ATTACKS? What should you do if your smartwatch flags high blood pressure? If your smartwatch warns you about possible high blood pressure, don't ignore it. But don't assume the watch has diagnosed you, either. The next step is to check your blood pressure using a validated upper-arm cuff. The American Heart Association recommends automatic upper-arm monitors for home measurements because they provide more reliable readings than typical wrist or finger monitors. If you're using Google's blood pressure trends feature and receive a "High" result, Google recommends checking your blood pressure twice a day for seven days and sharing those readings with your doctor. Make sure you follow your monitor's instructions and use the correct cuff size. Also, keep an eye on how you're feeling. If you experience emergency warning signs such as chest pain or difficulty breathing, seek immediate medical attention rather than waiting for another smartwatch assessment. And remember, even if your watch never sends an alert, you should continue getting your blood pressure checked. For another way to track your readings, see our article on how to monitor blood pressure with your Apple Watch using a compatible blood pressure monitor. The biggest challenge Google's smartwatch AI still faces One of my biggest questions about this technology comes down to how much confidence people will place in the results. Let's say your smartwatch tells you everything looks normal. Would you still bother checking your blood pressure? That's where the research raises an important concern. In Google's initial screening study, the AI missed a meaningful number of people who actually had hypertension. And while the results compared favorably with initial office screening, the study was relatively small. Researchers will need more evidence before the technology can become a dependable part of routine medical screening. Google's findings suggest that everyday wearables could eventually help identify people who might otherwise go undiagnosed. For now, though, a reliable blood pressure cuff and a conversation with your doctor remain essential. Kurt's key takeaways I like where Google is going with this. Most of us probably don't think about our blood pressure until we're sitting in a doctor's office with a cuff around our arm. So the idea that a smartwatch could spot a potential problem before we even know something's wrong is pretty exciting. But there's one number in this study that concerns me. The AI missed roughly one in three people who actually had high blood pressure. That's a lot, especially when you consider the serious health risks involved. I think this technology has tremendous potential, and I'm looking forward to seeing how Google improves it. But for now, I wouldn't rely on my smartwatch to tell me whether my blood pressure is normal. I'd still want to check it with a traditional cuff. Would you trust your smartwatch to warn you about high blood pressure? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com. articles.title: Kate Middleton Reveals She Never Rang the Bell After Cancer Treatment In New Documentary About Her Health
articles.summary: Catherine, Princess of Wales, never had her symbolic moment of ringing the bell to celebrate the completion of her cancer treatment, she reveals in “Heal,” a new documentary about her recovery.
articles.body: Catherine, Princess of Wales, never had her symbolic moment of ringing the bell to celebrate the completion of her cancer treatment, she reveals in a new documentary about her diagnosis and recovery. But the British royal may have marked that emotional milestone in her own way. In the trailer for her documentary “Heal,” the former Kate Middleton and her brother are seen in the middle of completing one of the United Kingdom’s toughest endurance challenges, a hiking feat called the National Three Peaks Challenge. “I didn’t ring the bell,” the Princess of Wales says to her brother, James Middleton, as they hike through the mountains. “Maybe this is your ringing of the bell,” he responds. The trailer for the surprise documentary was released over the weekend, revealing behind-the-scenes footage of Kate’s recovery from cancer and scenes of her conquering the hikes. The feat involves summiting the three highest peaks of Scotland, England and Wales, nearly 23 miles of hiking, within 24 hours. “Often it is through pain that we realize there’s a greater beauty that lies beyond that,” Kate says in a voiceover for the trailer. The documentary will air on NBC at 8 p.m. ET on Nov. 30 and stream on Peacock Dec. 1. “I think what this film does is allow her to tell the story in her own words,” NBC News royal contributor Emily Nash said on TODAY Nov. 23. “She has real agency over this story.” The trailer features a joyous moment when Kate’s daughter, Princess Charlotte, 11, rushes into her mother’s arms, followed by younger brother Prince Louis, 8, after Kate completed her journey. She then shares an embrace with husband Prince William and older son Prince George, 13, in rare video footage of the family together in private. “Healing is a journey,” she says in a voiceover in the trailer. “Helps you reconnect with the things you once knew and how to find a sense of hope and joy alongside uncertainty.” The seed for tackling the National Three Peaks Challenge was planted two years ago when she was in the hospital and James Middleton said they would one day achieve the feat together. “Seeing how far you’ve come is nothing short of inspiring,” James Middleton wrote on Instagram in July after they completed the summits. “Your strength, resilience, and determination, all while being the most amazing mother, wife, daughter, and sister, inspire me and so many others every single day. Keep being exactly who you are.” Kate also shared her own post on Instagram in June after conquering the challenge. “Healing, whether personal or collective, is not just about fixing what is wrong,” she wrote. “It is about finding balance in how we live. Between effort and acceptance, between control and trust, between thinking and simply being. Because in the end, bravery isn’t just about pushing forward. It is about knowing how to stay grounded, connected and present, no matter the terrain or landscape you are walking.” Her trek supported the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, which funds research and programs to support cancer patients during and after treatment, according to its website. The Princess of Wales has been in remission for nearly two years from an unspecified form of cancer. She and Prince William recently visited India for their first overseas trip since she publicly announced her diagnosis in March 2024.

articles.title: Fixing Alderney's air links an 'obsession' for politician
articles.summary: Steve Roberts says cancellations could pose "very real" risks to life and the economy.
articles.body:
A re-elected politician has said he is "obsessed" with fixing an island's air links after multiple flights were cancelled on election day.

Steve Roberts, who won one of the five available seats in the States of Alderney on Saturday , said he was "not surprised" by the cancellations as he felt services to the island had got "worse and worse".

He added he was concerned cancellations could present a "very real" risk to life if hospital appointments were missed.

Aurigny said the cancellations were due to a mixture of technical and weather-related issues and acknowledged the services had "fallen well short of expectations in recent months".

The States of Guernsey-owned airline has been criticised numerous times over the years, most recently from Alderney politicians in March when delays and cancellations left passengers stranded .

"I'm obsessed with improving these air links because they have never been so bad," Roberts told BBC Radio Guernsey.

"They are now becoming a real health risk to Alderney patients who are trying to get to the Princess Elizabeth Hospital [in Guernsey].

"The service has got that bad that no two days are the same, and no days give us a full service, ever."

Roberts, who has served on the States of Alderney since he was elected in May 2013, likened the struggle of getting urgent scans only to have flights cancelled as to living in "a Third World country".

He said he would soon present an independent report which detailing the problems Alderney could face if the disruptions were to continue.

"It's a report on the risk to life here, which is very, very real," said Roberts.

"There's risk to the economy, risk of hotels leaving and risk of the whole island really closing down, more or less."

Aurigny's chief commercial officer Philip Saunders said: "Aurigny recognises the air services to and from Alderney, which are operated by Skybus, have fallen well short of expectations in recent months.

"We regret the disruption and take the responsibility to deliver the service with the utmost seriousness."

articles.title: Dietitian Shares Her Favorite Canned Plant-Based Proteins
articles.summary: You might not realize just how good for you canned foods like beans really are. These plant proteins are simple, cheap and packed with nutrients, a dietitian says.
articles.body: Canned foods like beans are already pantry staples, but you might not realize just how good for you they are. And once you know, you might find yourself reaching for them a lot more often. “I’m a huge fan of canned plant-based proteins because they’re convenient, affordable and incredibly versatile,” says Natalie Rizzo, registered dietitian and TODAY nutrition editor. Among no-cook proteins, it doesn’t get much simpler or more nutritious than a can of beans or chickpeas. Plus, canned goods are cost-effective and have a long shelf life. “As a busy person, I rarely ever have time to soak and cook dried beans, so having canned options in the pantry means I can pull together a nutritious meal in just a few minutes,” Rizzo says. “And nutritionally, canned beans and legumes are still excellent sources of protein, fiber, vitamins and minerals.” Dietitian’s No. 1 Canned Plant-Based Protein Chickpeas Chickpeas are Rizzo’s go-to canned plant protein. They’re “probably my most-used canned protein,” she says, and “they’re incredibly versatile.” She likes to mash them into a sandwich filling, toss them into a salad, roast them for a crunchy snack or blend them into a dip. In one half-cup serving of chickpeas, you’ll find 7 grams of protein and a little more than 6 grams of fiber. And don’t just rinse away the liquid that canned chickpeas come in. That liquid is called aquafaba, Rizzo explains, “and it contains starches and proteins that give it some of the properties of egg whites.” You can whip aquafaba into a foam that can be used to add structure to vegan meringues, mousses and more. Try Rizzo’s Mediterranean Smashed Chickpea Wraps for an easy lunch that’s rich in both plant protein and fiber. Other Convenient Canned Plant Proteins Black Beans Another of Rizzo’s favorite canned plant proteins is black beans. All beans will provide some protein and fiber, but black beans are particularly high in both and naturally lend themselves to some of Rizzo’s favorite meals. You’ll find 8 grams of protein and 8 grams of fiber in just a half-cup serving of black beans. While canned beans do have more sodium than dry beans, “I don’t think people need to stress about that,” Rizzo says. Simply remove the canning liquid by draining the beans into a colander and rinsing them under cold water, she explains. That will significantly reduce the sodium. “They’re great for tacos, burrito bowls, quesadillas, soups, and homemade veggie burgers,” she says. Her Sweet Potato and Black Bean Quesadillas are a delicious, colorful way to use both beans and seasonal veggies to make a quick high-protein meal. Lentils Canned lentils are “a fantastic source of plant protein and fiber,” Rizzo says. Like the other beans and legumes on this list, lentils pack a filling combination of nutrients. A half-cup serving will net you a whopping 9 grams of plant-based protein and about 8 grams of fiber, which supports both gut and heart health. “I love adding them to soups, salads and pasta sauces,” Rizzo says. You can also use lentils to bulk up burger patties and add more nutrients to the meal.

articles.title: Who owns your body parts after surgery? Doctors uncover the complicated rules
articles.summary: Surgical patients are asking hospitals to hand over removed organs, teeth and joints as keepsakes, but pathology rules and release forms stand in the way.
articles.body: Most people want to forget their time in the operating room, yet some surgical patients insist on bringing their removed body parts home as souvenirs. While hospitals usually throw away removed tissue as medical waste, a small number of patients asks doctors to pack up their organs, teeth and worn-out joints after surgery, according to TIME magazine. Doctors say these patients want keepsakes for many reasons, from marking personal milestones to honoring cultural traditions. ORGAN HARVESTING BEGAN WHILE PATIENTS STILL SHOWED ‘SIGNS OF LIFE,’ FEDERAL INVESTIGATION FINDS Examples included a patient who kept her removed uterus in a jar after a hysterectomy as a reminder of the pain she survived, and another who dried her removed fallopian tubes to display in a box with flowers, according to the report. Other saved items included a pulled wisdom tooth fashioned into a calligraphy pen and a piece of medical tubing saved from a hospital stay and later given to a future spouse, the magazine said. Dr. Robyn Power, a gynecologic surgeon in South Florida, told TIME that only about five of her patients finished the paperwork to take tissue home over the past year, though more people are asking about it. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES She said patients living with painful conditions like endometriosis sometimes want the removed tissue as physical proof of what disrupted their lives. "It means something different to everybody," Power said. Hospital rules and safety Taking a body part home takes more than asking a surgeon in the recovery room.Dr. Kenneth Perry, an emergency room physician based in South Carolina, told Fox News Digital that rules surrounding who owns removed tissue vary widely. "As odd as it sounds, the ownership of tissue and other things removed from a person’s body is actually not settled law," Perry said. "Each state and each institution will have its own views on how to handle different tissues." CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES In the emergency room, Perry said doctors often let patients take home low-risk items like passed kidney stones, salivary gland stones or splinters, as long as the objects are not tied to a police case, like a bullet. Larger organs or body parts carry more risk because doctors must rule out infection or serious disease before releasing them. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "For instance, if an extremity or an organ has been removed due to infection or bleeding, it is often required that it goes through pathology testing to ensure it is safe," Perry said. He added that for pregnancy-related tissues, such as a placenta or remains from a miscarriage, hospitals typically have different rules and separate steps involved for families who ask to take them home. Patients debate the rules online Some surgical patients have taken to Reddit to share their confusion and experiences with trying to keep removed body parts. "Seeing as the hip bone is coming from my own body, I don't understand why I cannot," one user wrote ahead of a hip replacement in Washington State after a surgeon claimed that state law rejected his request to keep the bone. "My best friend's son got to keep one of his tonsils to take to school for show and tell," the user added. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Others pushed back, pointing to health hazards and hospital rules. "It's considered medical waste. Yes, bones can carry risks," one commenter wrote. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It really depends on the state laws, but most will not allow it," wrote another user who said they worked in pathology. "You can have a funeral home bury it if you like, but probably not take it home."

articles.title: GLP-1 Thanksgiving Survival Guide: What to Eat and Avoid If Taking Weight-Loss Drugs
articles.summary: GLP-1 weight-loss drugs can impact Thanksgiving as people find their appetite and digestion have changed. Doctors share foods to eat and avoid at dinner.
articles.body: The impact of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs will loom over many Thanksgiving dinner tables this holiday season as people find their appetite, body and digestion changed by the popular medications. About 11% of U.S. adults currently take a GLP-1 drug to lose weight, a new high, according to Gallup. One in five Americans with obesity are on the medication, suggesting “substantial” use of these drugs, researchers noted this month in a report published by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. GLP-1s slow stomach emptying and reduce appetite. People feel full and eat smaller meals, while avoiding certain foods, a strategy that can also reduce common side effects such as nausea and other gastrointestinal issues. But a Thanksgiving feast may complicate that routine, experts say. “Whenever we are around abundance of food, we’re more likely to eat more and maybe even more than we really even want to,” Dr. Melanie Jay, a professor at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine who leads the NYU Langone Comprehensive Program on Obesity, tells TODAY.com. GLP-1 patients who eat too much are more likely to experience reflux, nausea, vomiting or stomach discomfort, the doctor cautions. Then, there’s the psychological aspect of the drugs. Food-centric holidays like Thanksgiving or Christmas can feel strange when eating habits change. “Food is comfort, food is pleasure. So for some, there may be a feeling of loss if they can’t eat all the things they normally would,” Dr. Christopher McGowan, a gastroenterologist and obesity medicine specialist in Cary, North Carolina, previously told TODAY.com. A slimmer figure can also trigger comments from guests assembled at a Thanksgiving dinner, especially when family members haven’t seen each other for a while. “If you’re on a GLP-1 and you’ve lost a lot of weight, now you’re encountering all these family and friends who are going to have judgments about your body and about your medication. They are going to be asking about it. That can be a big stressor, too,” Jay says. So what’s the best way to feel as good as possible and enjoy yourself on Thanksgiving if you’re taking a GLP-1 weight-loss drug like Zepbound or Wegovy? The doctors had these tips. Enjoy the Foods You Love in Moderation Be intentional about what you eat, but it’s OK to indulge a bit, Jay says. The holiday and its signature foods come just once a year. “I don’t think Thanksgiving is the time to try to have an ideal plate. It’s a very special holiday for people,” she notes. “What are your favorite things? Start with those. Don’t deprive yourself of things you love… Don’t use this as the time to be super strict, and have some compassion for yourself.” If you crave a dish that might be on the list of foods to avoid while taking a GLP-1, eat a little bit of it just to get the taste, and eat mindfully, Jay advises. Nothing is off limits as long as it’s in moderation, McGowan said. Eat small portions and enjoy small bites. Be thankful for the opportunity to eat delicious food, but also make sure that you still feel good, Jay adds. Be Careful With Foods That Might Trigger Discomfort Take it easy with heavy, greasy foods, or those with lots of sugar. “Those are going to sit like a rock in your stomach and make you feel sick, (and) cause nausea,” McGowan said. Dishes that have a lot of fat or cheese can make people who take a GLP-1 feel worse, Jay adds. The proceed-with-caution list on Thanksgiving includes gravy, macaroni and cheese, buttery mashed potatoes, candied yams, stuffing and pie. “Focus on taking small portions and seeing how it sits with you before getting up for more,” Jay advises. “You know your body, and you know what you’re able to tolerate, especially if you’ve been on the meds for a while. If you’re new to the meds, then proceed with extra caution because you might be giving yourself a lot bigger dose of those fatty meals than you usually do,” says Jay, adding that you might feel sick afterward. Pay attention to satiety signals and don’t overindulge to the point of discomfort. Include Foods That Are Easy to Digest Good choices include the white meat of the turkey, a lean protein that’s recommended for GLP-1 users to protect muscle mass, and non-starchy vegetables like leafy greens. “If you’re agnostic (about) white meat or dark meat, the white meat might cause (fewer) problems for you because it’s not as fatty,” Jay says. Be Careful With Alcohol Many GLP-1 users find the drugs curb their desire to drink alcohol, so if they’re suddenly sipping more wine than usual at Thanksgiving dinner, it could be jarring. “People are not used to drinking as much because they’ve stopped drinking, and so when they start, they might find they can drink less than usual,” Jay says. “Also, it can worsen reflux disease and stomach upset. Some people say they can’t tolerate as much.” Don’t Skip a Dose of Your GLP-1 Medicine Some people might be tempted to skip a dose in order to have a bigger appetite and be able to eat more, but the experts warn against it. Stopping and restarting the drugs can cause even more side effects, Jay cautioned. “I would discourage the interruption of GLP-1 therapy for any reason,” McGowan said. “Instead of interrupting treatment so you can overindulge, let’s find ways to indulge in a healthy way.” Don’t Fast Before the Big Thanksgiving Dinner Don’t skip breakfast or lunch so you can eat more in the evening. “You don’t want to go in starving or feeling super hungry before Thanksgiving because then you’re more likely to eat too much and then overload your stomach at that point and feel sick,” Jay says. Prepare for GLP-1 Comments from Family People will notice changes in your body shape, weight or eating habits and might comment on them, so think about how you’ll handle questions or what you might say before the Thanksgiving get-together. “If it’s something that you’re excited to share, then share it,” Jay advised. “But I know there is a lot of stigma for some people around it, and you don’t have to talk about it if you don’t want to.” If other guests are commenting on what you’re eating, you can reply, “I’m trying to pace myself,” or “ I’m not that hungry,” she suggests. You can say in a friendly tone, “I’d rather not talk about my weight today,” and then change the subject. You might say, “Let’s talk about something else. How’s your family doing?” “There’s no reason you have to have a conversation about your weight management journey on GLP-1s with other people,” Jay says.

articles.title: As the US Loses Measles Elimination Status, These 7 Childhood Illnesses Could Also Come Back, Doctor Says
articles.summary: The U.S. lost its measles elimination status. An infectious disease doctor reveals what that indicates about the spread of other childhood illnesses as vaccination rates drop.
articles.body: Measles is officially endemic again. More than a quarter century after the U.S. celebrated eliminating the world’s most contagious virus, the Pan American Health Organization recently announced that the country has lost its measles elimination status. While the definition of “elimination,” according to the agency, varies by disease, measles is considered endemic again because the same strain has been circulating uninterrupted in the U.S. for more than a year. This setback comes as vaccination rates continue to drop and vaccine hesitancy continues to rise — which could mean that other preventable diseases Americans haven’t contended with in decades could also become more common. For the 2025-2026 school year, only 92.4% of kindergarteners received their measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine, a stat that’s been steadily decreasing since 2019-2020, according to data from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The recommended two doses of the MMR vaccine given in childhood are about 97% effective at preventing measles, but up to 95% percent of the population needs to be vaccinated to prevent widespread transmission, research shows. What’s more, an infection with measles can wipe the immune system’s memory of other germs, increasing the risk of infections that the person would’ve otherwise been protected against. As an infectious disease doctor, I believe these are the bacterial and viral illnesses that could reemerge the way measles has — and their hallmark signs to help you stay safe. Mumps Of all the infections vaccinated against in childhood, mumps may see a comeback first, as MMR immunization rates decline in the U.S. and other countries struggle with vaccination programs. While mumps has not been officially eliminated in the U.S., the CDC note that transmission has dropped by 99% since the mumps vaccination program started in 1967 — but it has started to rise again since 2006. There have been about 208 cases of mumps so far in 2026 (compared to 5,838 measles cases). Two shots of the MMR vaccine are 86% effective at preventing mumps. Unlike the measles and rubella components of the MMR shot, which typically provide lifelong protection, immunity from the mumps portion wears off over time, usually by college age. Mumps, a viral infection of the salivary glands beneath the ears, spreads via respiratory droplets from coughing, sneezing or talking, sharing items, or other close contact. Infected individuals are contagious a few days before their glands swell and up to five days after, according to the CDC. Appearing two to four weeks after exposure, symptoms begin with flu-like symptoms, such as fever, headache, muscle aches and fatigue, before progressing to the hallmark puffy cheeks and painful, swollen jaw. Most people recover within two weeks without any long-term problems, but the virus can cause severe inflammation in the reproductive organs, including the testicles, ovaries or breast tissue, and the brain. Rubella This childhood infection has been eliminated in the U.S. since 2004, according to the CDC, with fewer than 10 cases reported each year. A single dose of the MMR vaccine produces protective antibodies in about 95% of recipients, and with the two routine MMR doses, you can expect life-long immunity. This may be why I have never seen a case of rubella during or after my medical training. But I worry this could change. Rubella typically causes mild, cold-like symptoms — such as a low-grade fever, sore throat and swollen lymph nodes behind the ears, as well as pink eye — though up to 50% of infected people show no symptoms at all. For those who do, a telltale sign of rubella is a blotchy red rash that closely resembles measles. It starts on the face, spreads to the rest of the body within a day, and fades in the same order it appeared after three days. It’s often referred to as “three-day measles.” Rubella spreads through respiratory droplets when an infected person coughs or sneezes. People are contagious from one week before the rash appears until about one week after, so they can spread the virus before they know they are sick. Rubella poses the biggest risk to fetuses. Infection during pregnancy, especially in first trimester, can lead to serious birth defects, like heart, liver or spleen problems, loss of hearing and eyesight, and intellectual difficulties. Because there is no antiviral treatment, getting two doses of the MMR vaccine is the best way to prevent rubella. Chickenpox Before the chickenpox vaccine was introduced in 1995, there were about 4 million cases in the U.S. every year. Now, that number is less than 150,000. There are two types of chickenpox vaccines, one available in combination with MMR and one on its own. The hallmark symptom of chickenpox is a very itchy, highly contagious rash all over the body. Scratching can lead to a secondary infection, so see a doctor if the rash becomes warm, swollen or painful. What starts as red spots quickly turn into small, fluid-filled blisters, which eventually break open and form scabs. Because new spots continue to appear for several days, it’s common to have different lesions at different stages — spots, blisters, and scabs all at the same time, with some people getting as many as 500 blisters, according to the CDC. The illness usually lasts about a week. Once every blister has scabbed, the person can no longer spread chickenpox, and can go back to school or work. But even after you get better, the virus never fully leaves your body. Instead, it becomes dormant and hides inside your nerves. As we age, the virus can reawaken and cause a painful rash called shingles, most common in people 50 and older. Pertussis, aka Whooping Cough Cases of pertussis, also known as whooping cough, hit a decade high of 43,000 in the U.S. in 2024 due to broader testing, waning immunity and lower vaccination rates for the MMR and combined DTaP (diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis) vaccines. Before widespread vaccination, there were more than 200,000 cases a year in the U.S. Pertussis bacteria release toxins that damage the respiratory tract and cause the airways to swell. A week after exposure, people often develop symptoms that feel like a common cold, including a mild fever, runny nose and cough. In babies, the infection can lead to breathing difficulties. As the illness progresses, it can cause severe coughing fits, often to the point of vomiting, which can linger for more than two months. The cough is so intense that people make a high-pitched “whoop” sound when they gasp for air. Many people describe it as the worst cough of their lives. Whenever someone has a persistent, hacking cough lasting several weeks, pertussis is one of the first things I consider. Treatment requires starting antibiotics ideally before the coughing fits begin. No matter what, consult your doctor if you believe you have pertussis. Diphtheria Diptheria — a type of bacterial infection that damages the nose and mouth, and can lead to severe complications — has led to five or fewer cases in the U.S. every year since 1980. To maintain protection against diphtheria, adults should get a booster every 10 years; however, only about 60% of U.S. adults have done so in the past decade, data show. Diptheria spreads through respiratory droplets when an infected person coughs or sneezes, so people in close contact with an infected person are at the highest risk. Almost all diphtheria infections in the United States are linked to international travel. Symptoms typically appear several days after exposure, though some infected individuals experience no symptoms at all. Early signs include fever, sore throat and swollen glands. The most common symptom of diptheria is a thick, gray-white coating of dead tissue that forms in the throat. Neck glands can also become so swollen that it can difficult to breathe and swallow. Other complications also include heart muscle damage and kidney failure. Diphtheria is fatal in approximately 1 in 10 people, according to the CDC, even with medical care. Without treatment, up to half of those infected may die from the disease. Treatment requires antitoxin along with antibiotics. Tetanus Tetanus is a serious sickness caused by bacteria that live in dirt, dust and animal droppings, according to the CDC. Tetanus, which does not spread from person to person, remains rare in the United States, but the CDC’s provisional 2025 count of 38 cases was the highest since at least 2009. Open wounds that get dirty are typically breeding grounds for a tetanus infection. Trapped without air, these germs produce a toxin that attacks the nerves and forces the muscles to lock up, causing painful, uncontrollable spasms. The infection also causes an involuntary grin known as risus sardonicus, which happens when the facial muscles permanently contract. Over time, this can progress to respiratory failure as the muscles that help you breathe become exhausted. Polio Polio hadn’t spread in the U.S. since 1979. However, in 2022, a New Yorker caught it, likely from someone who’d been recently vaccinated with the oral polio vaccine, which isn’t commonly used in the U.S., suggesting they became infected outside of the country, TODAY.com previously reported. Their vaccine-derived infection led to the first polio-induced paralysis case in nearly a decade. Sewage tests later showed the virus was silently spreading across nearby New York counties. Now, as fewer children are getting routine vaccines, there is a higher chance polio could spread if someone brings it into the country from elsewhere. Polio is caused by a virus that affects the brain and spinal cord. Most people infected with polio have no symptoms, though some develop flu-like symptoms. In rare cases, it causes permanent paralysis, often in one arm or leg. Polio is very contagious and spreads from person to person when someone who is sick coughs, sneezes or breathes near you, or when you touch a surface contaminated with the virus. There is no cure, and vaccination is the only way to prevent it.

articles.title: Too young to be vaccinated for measles? Babies face growing threats from outbreaks
articles.summary: As measles outbreaks continue to soar, a new question has emerged: Should doctors give measles shots earlier to better protect babies?
articles.body: As measles outbreaks continue to soar nationwide, increasingly spilling from small, close-knit communities into the general population, a new question has emerged: Should doctors give measles shots earlier to better protect babies? Dr. Kristen Panthagani, an emergency medicine doctor in Connecticut, is worried about her baby, who has just turned 6 months old — too young for the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine that’s given after age 1. “I’ve been trying to figure out what to do to protect my son,” Panthagani said on her public health blog, called “You can know things.” He’s “in a tricky period when it comes to measles. He’s in a window of vulnerability where he likely doesn’t have protection against the virus.” Babies are born with antibodies against measles if their mothers have been vaccinated. But new evidence shows that protection doesn’t last as long as previously thought. “The assumption has always been that up until 6 months of age, babies are protected, and then from 6 to 12 months, there’s some waning,” said Dr. Buddy Creech, a pediatric infectious disease specialist and director of the Vanderbilt Vaccine Research Program at Vanderbilt University Medical Center. “That’s why we give the vaccine at 12 months.” New research from Creech’s team shows that protection is gone long before a child’s first birthday. Researchers analyzed blood samples from 92 mother-infant pairs and found that less than 20% of 6-month-old babies still have those protective antibodies. “By somewhere between 4 to 6 months of age, the majority of kids have completely lost the level of seroprotection that would be needed to protect against measles,” Creech said. He presented the research at an October meeting of the Infectious Diseases Society of America. It’s not been peer-reviewed. For more on the measles outbreak, read The Vaccine Divide, a data investigation into how the deadly virus is roaring back and childhood vaccine defenses continue to crack and crumble. Now that cases have exploded in the U.S., babies in that 6- to 11-month window are increasingly defenseless against the virus. “We’re going to have to rethink when we should give the first dose of measles vaccine,” Creech said. When should kids get their measles shots? For decades, the guidance was straightforward: Children receive their first MMR shot at 12 to 15 months old, followed by a second dose between ages 4 and 6. Together, the shots are 97% effective at protecting against measles, usually for life. In areas with active outbreaks, however, babies at 6 months old can get an early or “zero” MMR shot ahead of their two regular doses. And toddlers who’ve already had their first regular dose don’t have to wait until age 4 for their second shot. They’re eligible for the second dose 28 days after their first for maximum protection. Many parents in outbreak areas have taken advantage of the change in guidance. “We have seen huge uptake in the zero dose as well as in the early second dose,” Pennsylvania Secretary of Health Dr. Debra Bogen said last week during a briefing with the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials. More than 67,000 early MMR shots have been given in Pennsylvania since July, according to the state health department. The growing question now is whether those exceptions should become more widely used — or whether the routine vaccination schedule itself needs reconsideration — now that the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status. “There are people looking at this right now. They’re reviewing all of the latest science and seeing if the recommendation should change,” said Dr. Deanna Behrens, a Chicago-area pediatrician and secretary of the Illinois chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics. “We are on high alert.” As of Friday, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention had confirmed 5,838 cases, though the number is likely a vast undercount. More than 1,000 of those cases have been in kids under 5. About 17% of those children have needed hospitalization. Most kids recover from measles without a problem. But as the virus has caught fire across the U.S., doctors in outbreak zones have reported severe complications in some children, including trouble breathing, severe dehydration, pneumonia and brain swelling. Babies with measles are also at greater risk of developing a condition called subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, or SSPE, years after their infection. It’s almost always fatal. Twelve people have died of measles this year, according to state health departments. At least half of those deaths have been in babies or toddlers. The Vaccine Integrity Project, part of the University of Minnesota’s Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy, recently summarized the latest data on zero doses of MMR vaccine. The shot is 58% effective when given between 6 and 9 months, and 83% between 9 and 11 months. Side effects from the shots, such as fever and, rarely, febrile seizures, were the same in younger and older children. But there’s also evidence, the Vaccine Integrity Project’s review found, that the zero dose may impact how well kids’ immune systems respond to the two routinely recommended MMR shots. “It’s a trade-off right now,” said Dr. Heidi Moline, a pediatrician and clinical adviser to the Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy. “When there’s a significant amount of measles virus circulating, the short-term benefit of protection against measles outweighs the long-term lower antibodies.” As of now, there’s no indication the CDC is considering changes to the childhood vaccine schedule. The AAP said the group will review all of its immunization recommendations early next year. The CDC didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Vaccines recommended by the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices are generally free. There have been reports of health insurance claims being denied for early MMR vaccination, according to the AAP. “This is something the vaccine policy people are really going to have to look at,” said Dr. Peter Hotez, co-director of the Texas Children’s Hospital Center for Vaccine Development.
