articles.title: Does Scotland's NHS have a revolving door problem with senior managers?
articles.summary: The situation has been compared to "shuffling of deckchairs on the sinking Titanic" by the lawyer for an NHS whistleblower.
articles.body:
A recurring theme in the debate over the problems at NHS Grampian has been concern at a revolving door of senior managers in Scotland's NHS.

A damning report published earlier this month found that failures to learn from mistakes in Grampian had caused "repeated and avoidable harm" to patients.

Health Secretary Angela Constance has now sent in a team of four expert leaders to help drive urgent change by providing "external challenge, scrutiny and practical support".

But three of them previously held senior positions at other boards that also faced serious criticism.

Patient safety commissioner Karen Titchener has voiced "reservations" about those being asked to improve safety in one board when so many other boards had their own problems to solve.

And the lawyer representing a whistleblower who highlighted serious concerns at NHS Grampian has compared the situation in Scotland to "shuffling of deckchairs on the sinking Titanic".

Eyebrows have been raised about names on the health secretary's team of hand-picked experts who are being sent in to help with NHS Grampian's turnaround.

It is being led by Jim Crombie, deputy chief executive of NHS Lothian.

In 2018, as interim chief executive, he was forced to apologise after an independent investigation found a culture of "bullying and harassment" at the board.

Crombie also apologised for failings in 2024 after a whistleblowing report found mothers and babies had come to harm in the maternity unit at Edinburgh Royal Infirmary because of staff shortages and a toxic workplace culture.

Dr Chris Deighan, a former medical director at NHS Lanarkshire, is also on the team.

He was criticised recently by lawyers for the Scottish Hospitals Inquiry for being an unhelpful witness after he gave evidence on his role in the infection scandal at the Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Glasgow while he was at NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde.

A third rescue team member, Dr Pamela Johnston, was previously executive medical director at NHS Tayside.

In 2023, she apologised to patients after a review found senior managers at Ninewells Hospital had failed to adequately supervise disgraced neurosurgeon Sam Eljamel , despite a rising number of complaints.

The health secretary has said these external troubleshooters will work with NHS Grampian to turn things around.

She has given them six weeks, and has also made two appointments to the board.

Independent review ordered into surgery carried out by NHS Grampian

Surgeon calls for corporate homicide probe over claims patients unnecessarily bled to death

'Dramatic action' needed after NHS Grampian leaders criticised in damning report - Swinney

Meanwhile, Constance is sticking by Grampian chief executive Laura Skaife-Knight to get the job done - even though Skaife-Knight herself was found to have misled HIS over the way the death of a patient was investigated.

There are also questions about the performance of former bosses at NHS Grampian, with HIS referring to "long-standing" issues with culture and leadership in that executive team.

At the helm from 2020 to 2023 was Caroline Hiscox, who is now NHS Lothian chief executive - and being tipped to head one of two new super health authorities that would be formed if the government pushes forward with reforms to merge the mainland boards.

She was running NHS Grampian in 2022, at the time of a review into 19 avoidable patient deaths in surgery at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary, which was not made public.

Surgeon Dr Mohammed Habib, who leaked the report last week, said he was risking his job to speak out because he believed senior managers had tried to cover up what was going on.

His lawyer Aamer Anwar, a long-time ally of patient safety campaigners, says the current board and chief executive of NHS Grampian should go.

Anwar says there seems to be a permanent crisis in the NHS in Scotland, and people seem to have to accepted a "shuffling of deckchairs on the sinking Titanic, where you have one individual, who hasn't done a good job in one place, is then shuffled off to another place.

"They're all sitting on six-figure salaries so I don't expect the public to have any sympathy for their situation.

"They are just moved around and around in a very small circle, and everybody knows each other, so that causes concern."

On Tuesday, the health secretary is set to announce a review into how concerns over the surgical mortality rate at NHS Grampian were handled by the NHS and by the Scottish government.

Labour MP Dr Zubir Ahmed, who worked in Scotland for the majority of his career as a surgeon, said this must look at the relationship between politicians and senior NHS management.

In an interview with Radio Scotland Breakfast , he said: "It doesn't sit right with me that in NHS Scotland we don't get much of a turnover of senior managers, they move from one place to the next."

Dr Ahmed said getting "the right people in the right jobs" was very important.

Former SNP MSP Alex Neil, who served as health secretary between 2012 and 2014, said there was "too much of the same people doing a job swap almost on a rotational basis" within the NHS.

"I think we need to bring in fresh blood from outside - either outside the health service in terms of management, or outside the country."

We asked the Scottish government about these concerns and about the choice of experts sent in to help with improvements at NHS Grampian.

In response, a spokesperson stressed that leadership and accountability for NHS Grampian rested with the chief executive and the health board.

"This is not a leadership team," they said.

"This is an intervention support team which is providing broad external support in organisational and operational recovery, clinical governance, patient safety and performance to support NHS Grampian's improvement. It will not be making decisions.

"The health secretary has been clear she welcomes the involvement of the patient safety commissioner in scrutinising the progress NHS Grampian must make, and we understand she is due to visit Grampian this week."

Constance has decided that the situation at NHS Grampian does not meet the "exceptional circumstances" needed for direct ministerial intervention in the running of the board.

Such a step - known as stage five in the government's escalation framework - has only ever been used once, in Tayside in 2018.

Instead, Grampian will remain at stage four, where it has been since May 2025 due to issues around finances, leadership and governance.

NHS Ayrshire and Arran is also at stage four for financial management, governance and leadership.

That means external support is being provided by a government-appointed "assurance board" at senior levels because the health board leadership has been unable to deliver improvements.

The NHS boards in Borders, Dumfries and Galloway, Highland, Lothian, Orkney and Tayside are all at stage three for different reasons.

This means tailored support and scrutiny is provided by the government because of "risks materialising".

The rest are at level two, with increased monitoring by central government - but none are at stage one, where they would be delivering in line with expectations.

In total, that means eight of the 14 regional health boards in Scotland have some level of government direct intervention at level three or above.

articles.title: Alzheimer’s risk jumps 53% for millions living with common blood sugar condition
articles.summary: New research suggests people with type 2 diabetes face a 53% higher risk of developing Alzheimer's disease, with experts pointing to blood sugar control.
articles.body: People living with type 2 diabetes may face a significantly higher risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease compared to those without the condition, a new study suggests. Researchers from Curtin University's School of Population Health in Australia reviewed 40 observational studies including people with Alzheimer’s disease and type 2 diabetes. After accounting for other health and lifestyle factors, the researchers found that individuals with this condition have a 53% higher risk of developing Alzheimer's. That translates to roughly 4.7 new cases for every 1,000 people tracked over a year. 3 THINGS TO AVOID IN MIDDLE AGE COULD MEAN 13 MORE YEARS WITHOUT DEMENTIA, STUDY FINDS "It doesn't add newer experiments or show that diabetes directly causes Alzheimer's disease, but how we should read it is that someone with diabetes has about one and a half times more chance of getting Alzheimer's disease compared to someone without it," Dr. Caghan Kizil, professor of neurological sciences at Columbia University Department of Neurology, who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital. The findings were published in the journal Alzheimer’s Research & Therapy on Nov. 9. ALZHEIMER’S BLOOD MARKER COULD PREDICT COGNITIVE DECLINE RISKS, MAYO CLINIC SAYS Unlike earlier reviews that often combined different forms of diabetes and dementia, the new analysis looked specifically at type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer’s disease to calculate the rate of new cases, according to lead study author Dr. Emmanuel Adewuyi, a researcher at the Curtin School of Population Health. "Reporting both relative risk and incidence measures helps explain not only whether risk is higher, but how frequently new cases occur," Adewuyi told Fox News Digital. "What stood out was the fuller picture that emerged when we examined how often Alzheimer’s disease developed alongside how risk compared between groups." Experts point to a few key ways that poor blood sugar control harms brain cells over time. POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY PREVENT PREDIABETES FROM TURNING INTO DIABETES Excess blood sugar can stiffen and narrow blood vessels in the brain, causing a decrease in blood flow and oxygen to brain cells, according to Dr. Nikhil Palekar, director of Stony Brook Medicine's Center of Excellence for Alzheimer's Disease in New York. "Insulin resistance prevents the brain cells from utilizing glucose, resulting in reduced cellular energy and neuronal functions," Palekar, who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital. Maintaining optimal blood sugar levels can reduce the risk for Alzheimer’s, the doctor confirmed. "GLP-1 agonists have been shown to lower elevated blood sugar levels as well [as] decrease brain inflammation, which is a risk factor for Alzheimer’s disease," Palekar said. Limitations of the analysis There were some limitations, including extreme variation across the studies. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Because the individual studies reported vastly different rates — ranging from fewer than one to nearly 30 new cases per 1,000 people each year — the researchers could not pinpoint a single, exact risk rate. Additionally, the analysis relied on real-world observational data rather than controlled clinical trials. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "Importantly, these are population-level findings," Adewuyi said. "They cannot predict whether a particular person will develop Alzheimer’s disease." Variations in where the studies were conducted, how long patients were tracked and which outside health factors were considered all influenced the outcomes. Alzheimer's is one of the most prevalent dementia types, comprising almost 70% of all cases, Kizil noted, which is why the studies are heavily focused on that condition. However, as diabetes can deprive the brain of essential nutrients, it can contribute to a wide range of neurological diseases beyond just Alzheimer’s. Lowering the risk For people who have diabetes along with an increased risk of developing dementia, Kizil recommends undergoing cognitive screenings much earlier, alongside blood sugar control and other measurements. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ People with diabetes or any type of cardiovascular risk factors, including high blood pressure, should work proactively with their doctors on metabolic control and earlier cognitive monitoring, he advised. Adewuyi emphasized that the study provides no basis for changing medication or adopting tighter blood glucose targets specifically to prevent Alzheimer’s disease. "If someone notices persistent changes in memory or thinking – particularly if these are affecting medicines, glucose monitoring or daily activities – they should discuss them with their healthcare team," he advised. The early signs and symptoms of Alzheimer’s are most often related to becoming more forgetful, according to Palekar. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Some of those include "short-term memory loss, such as forgetting recent events or conversations, misplacing things routinely, having difficulty managing finances or performing complex daily tasks," the doctor told Fox News Digital. To support brain health, Palekar recommends following a primary care physician’s guidance to closely monitor blood sugar levels alongside key lifestyle modifications — "specifically, moderate-intensity aerobic exercise 150 minutes a week and a balanced diet, such as the Mediterranean diet."

articles.title: Flight Delayed? A Trainer Shares 5 Easy Exercises to Do While Stuck at the Airport
articles.summary: In TODAY.com’s Expert Tip of the Day, a trainer shares 5 simple exercises you can do at the airport to boost circulation, ease joint stiffness and reduce stress.
articles.body: If you’re one of the millions of Americans planning to travel by air for the holidays, there’s a decent chance you may encounter flight delays or cancellations. Between severe weather, system outages and ground stops, air travel seems more chaotic than ever lately. These disruptions leave many passengers stressed and stranded in terminals. When you’re stuck at the airport, it can be tempting to sit and doom scroll or find the nearest bar to blow off steam. However, moving your body is one of the best ways to keep busy before your flight, says Start TODAY trainer and TODAY contributor Stephanie Mansour. A little exercise can help you feel better, inside and out, on the worst of travel days. Fitness Tip of The Day: Try These Simple Exercises When You’re Stuck at the Airport It can be hard to prioritize fitness on busy travel days. “I often find myself at the airport having scrambled to get out the door and forgoing my workout,” says Mansour. So if you find yourself with extra time to kill due to flight delays or a long layover, try squeezing in a mini workout with these 5 simple, airport-friendly exercises: Elevated runner’s lunge stretchSeated glute stretchSquatsLifting bagsWalking briskly Why It Matters Moving your body before a flight — whether it’s stretching, strength training or walking — has physical and mental benefits, says Mansour. Stretching the legs, glutes and lower back can help ease tension and stiffness from sitting for long periods. Bodyweight exercises, such as squats, get your heart pumping, build strength and combat dead butt syndrome. In lieu of lifting weights, you can pick up your carry-on for an arm workout. Walking is an easy, accessible cardio exercise to move the body and combat boredom while stuck in airport limbo. “I’ve been encouraging my clients for decades to get more steps in at the airport,” says Mansour. “Walking for just five minutes can give you a boost of feel-good endorphins, get your heart rate up, improve circulation, burn calories and just make you feel good before sitting for a long time on the plane,” she explains. All of these airport exercises can also reduce travel-related stress and anxiety. “Mentally, you’re focusing on the present moment with your body,” says Mansour. How to Get Started You can perform all five exercises as part of a full-body routine, or try one or two depending the time you have and your energy levels. “I like to find an empty (boarding) area...and use a chair as if it was a bench at the gym,” says Mansour. Elevated runner’s lunge: With your back to the chair, put one foot up on a chair and bend into the front knee, stretching the back legs and hip flexors into an elevated runner’s lunge. Hold for up to one minute, breathing deeply, and switch sides.Seated glute stretch: Sit down on the seat and cross your right ankle over the left knee, flexing the right foot and leaning forward to stretch the right glute. Hold for 30-60 seconds and switch sides. Squats: Do 10 regular squats while looking out the window at the planes. To make it more challenging, stand with your legs wider than shoulder width, turn your toes out, and do 10 more sumo squats.Lifting bags: Use your carry-on bag or backpack as a makeshift weight and do 5–10 bicep curls or rows. Walking: Walk at a brisk pace (3–4 miles per hour) for 15–30 minutes around the terminal, or try interval walking. “I also encourage people to tie a gratitude practice to their workout to help them focus on being positive rather than worried or stressed about delays,” says Mansour. TODAY’s Expert Tip of the Day series is all about simple strategies to make life a little easier. Every Monday through Friday, different qualified experts share their best advice on diet, fitness, heart health, mental wellness and more.

articles.title: The No. 1 Warning a Doctor Gives About Over-the-Counter Painkillers
articles.summary: Dr. Trisha Pasricha, a gastroenterologist, says taking too many NSAIDs is more common than you think. She breaks down the complications that can occur.
articles.body: TODAY’s Never Have I Ever series offers guidance about procedures and practices our trusted health experts would never participate in. Discover why they should be avoided and which healthy practices you should turn to instead. If you’ve got a migraine, fever, stomachache or lower back pain, chances are you have just what you need in your medicine cabinet to reduce the discomfort— a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID), such as ibuprofen or aspirin. These are “really common meds that we can often use for day-to-day minor aches and pains,” gastroenterologist and author, Dr. Trisha Pasricha, tells TODAY.com. And why wouldn’t you use them? “They are convenient. They are cheap. You get them over the counter, and they work really well,” she adds. They work by blocking the body from producing inflammatory compounds called prostaglandins that, when they build up, hurt. While helpful when taken in the proper amount, NSAIDs can be dangerous if used too often or at too high a dose, Pasricha says. Never Have I Ever: Taken Too Many NSAIDs “When they’re taken in large quantities, (NSAIDs) can damage the lining of the gut,” explains Pasricha. “And, in some cases, they can cause bleeding and ulcers.” She describes it as a “slippery slope.” Take knee pain that doesn’t resolve after a dose of NSAIDs. You might take just one more capsule or pill to make it through the day. Then, you realize you’ve started menstruating and take a different NSAID for cramps. It’s a common mistake, she says. As many as 15% of people exceed their ibuprofen dose limit, research found. Then, what began as knee pain and monthly cramps could land you in the hospital for gastrointestinal distress too. What to Do Instead While it’s typically safe to use NSAIDs, Pasricha says to follow the instructions on the bottle for details about how many pills you should take, how often and what the daily limit is. Take the NSAID at the first onset of pain, says Pasricha. Rather than hoping the pain will get better on its own or waiting until it’s debilitating, opt for the NSAID first thing. This plan will keep you from overdoing it on painkillers later. Plus, Pasricha adds, “the enzymes actually work better when you take them early and give them a good chance to stop the (pain) at the source,” rather than letting the prostaglandins build up. Pasricha also recommends sticking to one type of NSAID because some have the same active ingredient. So, while you might be taking one brand-name NSAID to address a migraine and another for muscle soreness, you may not realize you’re taking the same medication in a different package, thus significantly increasing your dosage and chances of gut issues. Finally, if you find yourself turning to NSAIDs regularly to address persistent pain, talk to your doctor, says Pasricha. While they make us less aware of pain, it’s important to remember that NSAIDs don’t cure or treat. Regular or long-lasting discomfort will likely require a diagnosis and treatment plan.

articles.title: ACS (health) orders rectification of new 500-bed Dumka hospital flaws in 30 days
articles.summary: ACS Dr Ajoy Kumar Singh inspects Dumka’s new 500-bed PJMCH hospital, flags flaws, orders fixes in 30 days; capacity to rise to 800 beds.
articles.body: Dumka: Additional chief secretary (ACS) of the health department-cum-development commissioner, Dr Ajoy Kumar Singh, on Tuesday checked the infrastructure, construction quality, and facilities available at the newly built 500-bed hospital at the Phulo Jhano Medical College and Hospital (PJMCH), Dumka.The inspection revealed several technical and structural shortcomings. A lecture hall, meant for 120 students, had only 112 seats.He ordered an examination of the role of the consultant associated with the hospital’s construction and design and directed the construction agency to ensure rectification of the deficiencies within a month.“The new 500-bed facility would be integrated with the existing 300-bed Sadar Hospital and operated through the medical college, raising the combined capacity to 800 beds. The health department would appoint the required doctors, lecturers and faculty members,” Singh said.A special team, led by the deputy development commissioner, would inspect every building structure, facility, room, and submit a detailed report, the ACS added.The medical college campus, spread over around 25 acres, would be expanded to more than 100 acres in accordance with the chief minister’s directions. The district administration has provided the required land. The govt also plans to increase MBBS seats from 100 to 200 over the next three years and introduce postgraduate courses from next year, with a target of 150 PG seats, said Singh.Stay updated with the latest Ranchi news. articles.title: Commuter injures himself with blade on Virar-Churchgate local
articles.summary: Commuter Praful Jhade injured himself with a blade on a Virar-Churchgate local; train halted at Andheri, police aided him, services unaffected.
articles.body: Mumbai: A commuter injured himself with a blade inside a Virar-Churchgate local train on Monday evening, scaring fellow passengers. People pulled the emergency chain to stop the train at Andheri station.The incident occurred after the train left Virar around 6 pm. The commuter, identified as Praful Jhade, was sleeping on a seat when another passenger asked him to get up. Jhade then took out a blade kept in his hair and began slashing himself, leaving fellow commuters alarmed.The train halted at platform 7 of Andheri station at 6.56 pm. A woman police constable, Saraswati, and Maharashtra Security Force personnel inspected the coach and found Jhade injured. He was taken to the station’s emergency medical room, where doctors administered first aid.During questioning, Jhade told the railway police that he was a resident of Nagpur and was undergoing treatment for a mental health condition at JJ Hospital here. He attributed his actions to stress arising from family-related issues.The police searched him but did not find the blade. After receiving first aid and recording his statement, Jhade left for home on his own. articles.summary: 25-year-old scooty rider Ajay Patil died in Mumbai’s Kurla after crashing into a tempo while overtaking a BEST bus; police probe underway.
articles.body: Mumbai: A 25-year-old scooty rider, Ajay Gunavant Patil, died after colliding with a tempo while allegedly trying to overtake a BEST bus in Kurla (W) on Tuesday morning.Police said the accident occurred at 7.10am in Budh Colony and caused a traffic jam lasting beyond 9am.The bus, operating on route 310/39 from Bandra Terminus East to Kurla West bus station, was passing through the area when Patil allegedly tried to overtake it from the right. His scooty collided with a tempo moving ahead of the bus, causing him to lose balance and fall onto the road between the bus’s front and rear wheels, police said. Patil suffered severe head injuries and was taken to Rajawadi Hospital, where doctors declared him dead.Senior BEST officials and the wet-lease operator’s representatives inspected the accident spot. articles.title: Tyson Fury Reveals Schizophrenia Diagnosis and Recalls Hearing Voices Ahead of Anthony Joshua Fight
articles.summary: Tyson Fury and his wife, Paris, describe his diagnoses of schizophrenia and bipolar disorder in the new Netflix documentary Tyson Fury. The boxer, 38, recall...
articles.body:
Tyson Fury and his wife, Paris, describe his diagnoses of schizophrenia and bipolar disorder in the new Netflix documentary Tyson Fury . The boxer, 38, recalls a severe mental health crisis that interrupted his career.

The crisis followed his November 2015 victory over Wladimir Klitschko in Düsseldorf, which made him unified world heavyweight champion. He withdrew from a planned rematch after being declared medically unfit to fight.

Fury had already publicly discussed bipolar disorder in an October 2016 interview, as BBC Sport reported at the time.

Directed by Lucy Wilcox, the feature includes interviews with Fury's father, John, and previously unseen archive footage. It traces the boxer's childhood and family life alongside his career.

Netflix Documentary Revisits Fury's Frightening Hospital Stay

In June 2016, Fury was taken to a hospital with a suspected heart attack. Paris says doctors told her he had experienced an anxiety attack.

During his stay, Fury recalls believing the radio was speaking to him and hearing voices threatening him and his family. He describes being frightened that he would need long-term psychiatric hospitalization.

"Words can't explain the darkness I was in," he says in the film, according to Sky Sports .

Fury also recalls seeking help from a psychiatrist in London as his anxiety became overwhelming. He says she questioned him extensively, identifying depression, anxiety and bipolar disorder.

Paris Says She Struggled to Understand the Diagnoses

Paris recalled her initial confusion over the schizophrenia diagnosis in excerpts published by The Independent . She acknowledged that her understanding of the condition had been shaped by misconceptions.

She was also unfamiliar with bipolar disorder. Once medical professionals explained it, she said, she began to recognize the difficulties her husband had been experiencing.

A Halloween Night Helped Prompt His Boxing Comeback

Fury identifies Halloween 2017 as a turning point. In a documentary account quoted by ITV News , he recalls going out in a glow-in-the-dark skeleton costume, hoping he would not be recognized.

Seeing younger people in the bar prompted him to reflect on his drinking and the opportunities he felt he had lost. He had gained substantial weight during his absence and was struggling with drug and alcohol addiction.

He began training with Ben Davison and working with promoter Frank Warren, returning to the ring in June 2018 against Sefer Seferi.

His December 2018 fight with Deontay Wilder ended in a draw. Fury won their February 2020 rematch by seventh-round stoppage to claim the WBC heavyweight title.

Fury and Joshua Will Finally Meet in Cardiff

Tyson Fury premieres on November 27, two weeks before the December 11 event that Netflix will stream globally from Principality Stadium in Cardiff, Wales.

Fury and Joshua appeared at a London press conference on September 30, posing for their first official face-off. The two former heavyweight champions have never faced each other in a professional bout, and Fury enters the matchup after defeating Arslanbek Makhmudov by unanimous decision in April 2026.

Fury told The Guardian that he worries about finding purpose after boxing, saying everyday routines alone would not be enough.
